blocks.text: “I declare,” he says, “I say this with complete seriousness. Until this crime is solved and punished by law, I almost feel a stain on my name. This gentleman gave a large part of his life to serving me. He gave the last day of his life to serving me. He often ate at my table and slept under my roof. He leaves my house to go to his own. Within an hour of leaving my house, he is struck down. He may have been followed from my house. He may have been watched at my house. He may even have been chosen as a victim because of his connection with my house. That connection may have made him seem richer and more important than his quiet manner suggested. I have money, influence, and a high position in society. If I cannot use these to discover everyone who took part in this crime, I fail. I fail to show my respect for that gentleman's memory. I fail to show my loyalty to someone who was always loyal to me.”

He makes this strong declaration with deep feeling and great seriousness. He looks round the room as if he were speaking to a large gathering. Mr. Bucket glances at him with a serious, watchful expression. There might even be a little pity in that look—if thinking such a thing were not so bold.

“Today's ceremony,” Sir Leicester continues, “clearly showed how much the finest people in the land respected my dead friend.” He stresses the word ‘friend’, for death removes all differences in rank. “That ceremony has, I say, made my shock still greater. This crime was most horrible and showed a shocking lack of fear. If my own brother had committed it, I would not spare him.”
Mr. Bucket looks very serious. Volumnia says that the dead man was the most trusted and dearest person!
“You must feel his death as a great loss, miss,” Mr. Bucket replies gently. “No doubt about that. He was the sort of person whose death would be a great loss. I'm sure he was.”

Volumnia replies that she has a sensitive mind. She has firmly decided that she will never recover from this loss while she lives. Her nerves will never be calm again, and she has no hope of ever smiling again. Meanwhile, she folds a letter into the shape of a three-cornered hat. It describes her sad condition and is for that old general at Bath, who inspires such fear and respect.
“It gives a delicate woman a shock,” says Mr. Bucket with sympathy, “but the feeling will pass.”

More than anything, Volumnia wants to know what is being done. Are they going to find that dreadful soldier guilty, or whatever they call it? Did he have any helpers in the crime, or whatever the law calls them? She asks many more equally innocent questions.

“Well, you see, miss,” Mr. Bucket replies, moving his finger to help persuade her. He is so naturally polite to women that he almost calls her ‘my dear’. “It isn't easy to answer those questions at this moment. Not at this moment. I've worked on this case morning, noon, and night, Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet.” Mr. Bucket brings him into the conversation because of his importance. “Without a glass or two of sherry, I don't think I could have kept my mind working so hard. I could answer your questions, miss, but my duty does not allow it. Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, will very soon hear everything we have found out. And I hope he may find it”—Mr. Bucket looks serious again—“satisfactory.”

The weak cousin only hopes some fellow will be executed—to set an example. Thinks more influence is needed—to get a man hanged these days—than to get a man a job paying ten thousand a year. Has no doubt—to set an example—far better to hang the wrong fellow than no fellow at all.
